baseline.answer: The authors propose the LLM-as-a-judge approach to automate the human evaluation of chat assistants. They expect it to work because strong LLMs, such as GPT-4, can achieve an agreement rate of over 80% with human experts, which is comparable to the level of agreement among human evaluators. This establishes a foundation for an effective automated evaluation method that can enhance chatbot quality and user experiences [llm_as_judge_mtbench, p.9].

The main advantages of LLM-as-a-judge, according to the MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena paper, include its scalability and ability to approximate human preferences effectively, achieving over 80% agreement with human evaluations. This method serves as a promising alternative to traditional human evaluations, which are costly and laborious. Additionally, LLM-as-a-judge can swiftly evaluate both the core capabilities and human alignment of models by combining capability-based benchmarks with preference-based benchmarks [llm_as_judge_mtbench, p.2].

DPO differs from the PPO-based RLHF pipeline used in InstructGPT by bypassing the need to fit an explicit reward and perform reinforcement learning (RL) to learn the policy. Instead, DPO uses a single maximum likelihood objective, which allows it to optimize the parametric model directly without the complexities associated with actor-critic algorithms like PPO. Self-RAG differs from conventional RAG in that it enables retrieval on demand and selection of the best possible model output via fine-grained self-reflection. While conventional RAG processes retrieved passages in a more straightforward manner, Self-RAG concurrently processes multiple retrieved passages, evaluates their relevance, and generates corresponding task outputs. It also generates critique tokens to criticize its own output and choose the best one based on factuality and overall quality, which is not a feature of conventional RAG [self_rag, p.0].

RAPTOR differs from traditional RAG by using a recursive tree structure that captures both high-level and low-level details about a text. It clusters chunks of text, generates summaries of those clusters, and builds the tree from the bottom up. This allows RAPTOR to load into an LLM’s context chunks representing the text at different levels, enabling it to effectively and efficiently answer questions at varying levels of granularity. In contrast, traditional RAG typically does not utilize such a multi-layered structure for indexing and retrieval [raptor, p.0].
